rationale: This case study of Trinidad analyzes residential flat-rate water charges based on the annual rateable value of property (ARV), cost-recovery rules, and implicit subsidies (`fees_tariffs_subsidies`), while secondarily discussing public water utility governance and fiscal autonomy (`regulatory_model_ownership`). Empirically, the paper evaluates multiple co-equal outcome dimensions resulting from this pricing regime (`assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple`: `multiple`), led by widespread service intermittency, rationing, and declining potability (`effective_access`), alongside regressive household expenditure shares (`economic_access`), lack of network expansion in poor settlements (`primary_connection`), and utility revenue shortfalls/unaccounted-for water (`administrative_outcome`). Methodologically, it is a qualitative institutional/policy case study combining review of utility accounts and consultant reports (1988-2008) with key stakeholder and decision-maker interviews conducted in 1993, 2000, 2002, and 2010 (`qualitative`).
